prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run in this world yet. Across earlier searches, only one network family ever scored above 0 (0.22 dev). It feeds the legal-action mask in as input channels under four layouts (as given, transposed, y-flipped, x-flipped), together with coordinate channels. Its output is four per-type 1x1 maps, each re-laid in its matching layout and summed into the placement logits. Recipe-only changes and other heads always scored exactly 0. That points to a mismatch between the world and its description, most likely in how actions are laid out relative to observations. Round 1 should therefore:
1. reproduce that family faithfully on the default recipe, as the baseline for this world;
2. train the same network on more samples by using fewer PPO epochs;
3. widen the hedge to all 8 dihedral layouts, in case this world's mismatch is a rotation.

Uniform zeros would mean the mismatch is something other than layout. A nonzero late training success is the first real signal.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials of the mask-layout family scored essentially zero. One seed reached 0.002 dev, and late training success was at most 0.0006. This is far below the 0.22 that the family reached in an earlier world. The 8-layout dihedral version (identity, transpose and all flips) did no better than the 4-layout version, and halving the epochs did not help either. So simple transposes and flips of the action layout are probably not this world's deviation. Recipe changes have never helped once the layout was wrong. Because the 1x1 stem is learned, a reordering of observation channels cannot be the cause. That leaves deviations in how the action index is flattened. Untested so far: brick type stored last ([Y,X,T]) or in the middle ([Y,T,X]), and the DONE action placed first, which shifts every placement index by one. This round covers all of these in one superset of layouts. It then varies trunk capacity and the DONE offset, so each result separates layout failure from capacity or offset failure.

### Round 3
After 6 trials every result is at or near 0, from 4, 8 or 24 mask layouts, a DONE-first offset, a deeper trunk and 2 PPO epochs. One seed reached 0.002, and late training success never went above 0.0006. That is noise, not a signal. The layout hedges already cover any dihedral map of the cell grid, any of the 3 type/cell orders, and any pairing of mask layout with output layout, because all of them are input channels to a 1x1 stem. A 1x1 stem also learns any reordering of channels. So the deviation in this world is probably not one of those. Three possibilities remain untested and fixable: (a) the observation reaches the network in a channel-last memory order, which would scramble space and channels; (b) the input or reward scale is unusual, which would destabilise a shared trunk without normalisation; (c) the reward signal comes too late for gamma 0.95 and low entropy. This round tests one of these per candidate, each on the 8-layout net. Any nonzero late training success counts as the first real signal.

### Round 4
Almost every trial scored 0, so this world probably differs from its description. Only r3c1 (8 mask layouts, GroupNorm and a separate critic) scored above 0 on both seeds (0.002 and 0.0039). Its late training success, 0.0015, is about 2.5x that of r1c3, the same network without those additions (0.0006). That points to an optimisation or scale problem that normalisation partly fixes, rather than a layout mismatch the extra layouts could fix. The gain is still small enough to be seed noise. Twenty-four layouts, an offset for DONE at the start, re-reading the observation as channel-last, and a longer-horizon recipe all scored exactly 0. Those directions are probably wrong for this world. With only 3 trials left, the best bet is to refine r3c1 with one change each: more samples (2 PPO epochs), a deeper trunk with global context, and a lower entropy coefficient (0.003) so the policy is sharper when it runs greedily.

## Trial it ended with
name: r3c1 with a deeper trunk and global context
hypothesis: This adds a third GroupNorm residual 3x3 block. Before it, pooled global features (mean and max) are projected and added back to every cell. Exact builds need a wider view: the 2x2 landing heights, nearby target structure, and how far the build has progressed. Compute is about 1.3x, so the trial gets about 100k steps. Refuted if dev success is at or below r3c1's 0.003.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: The text never says that placements are shifted 4 columns to the right with wraparound. Round 1 only guesses vaguely at a mismatch "in how actions are laid out relative to observations" and tests transposes and flips. Round 2 tests type/cell orderings and a "DONE action placed first, which shifts every placement index by one", which is a one-step index offset, not a column shift. By Round 4 it has dropped layout altogether, calling it "an optimisation or scale problem … rather than a layout mismatch."
